articles.title: Platform Traffic Collapse Hits Reddit and Google Search
articles.content: This is a column about AI. My fiancé works at Anthropic. See my full ethics disclosure here . On Thursday afternoon, Demis Hassabis celebrated a milestone for Google’s AI efforts: Gemini 4 Carbon, a new large language model that is currently available only to cyber defenders, topped Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. After a series of delays in new model releases and a growing perception that the company is falling off the frontier, early signs suggest that Carbon marks a return to form. For Alphabet’s chief scientist, the news surely felt like a vindication.  Investors, however, are much less certain. On the same day, Google’s parent company had its worst day in history as a public company. Alphabet’s stock fell 12.6 percent, erasing around $500 billion in market value. The loss marked the second-biggest stock market plunge ever, following Nvidia’s $593 billion slide in January 2025. And it was Google’s biggest one-day decline since the great financial crisis. Most of the selloff came from investor worries about the huge scale of Google’s AI infrastructure buildout. The company plans to spend up to $205 billion on capital expenses this year, and has promised to spend even more in 2027. And it reported free cash flow of negative $9 billion — an acceleration of a decline that began the previous quarter. Ordinarily I don’t pay much attention to one-day dips in a stock price, no matter how large. (Nvidia stock now trades more than 10 percent above where it did in January.) But on an earnings call, Google’s chief business officer offered a newsworthy answer to an analyst who questioned why the company’s search revenue growth was slowing despite the fact that queries are increasing. Among the reasons, said Philipp Schindler, is that increased usage of Google’s AI Mode is hurting the company because it makes less money than traditional search .  Then, a few hours later, Reddit reported its own earnings for the quarter — and saw its own stock drop 15 percent . The company noted that its traffic from search had fallen meaningfully, and that by the fourth quarter daily users might decline by a low double-digit percentage. As a result, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said in a shareholder letter, the company would increasingly push users to log in to use the site. After decades of letting people (and bots) browse the site for free, they would now have to create accounts. “It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally,” Huffman said . “It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.” Google has long pushed back against claims that AI answers are bad for the web by saying that they encourage people to conduct deeper, more expansive searches that result in higher-quality clicks to websites. Today’s news suggests that narrative is falling apart: advertisers are getting less from AI Mode than they get from traditional search, and so is a big publisher like Reddit.  But while it’s tempting to accuse Google of a strategic misstep here, in the end I suspect it will come out ahead. And while the web and its publishers will continue to struggle, Google will mostly be able to dismiss that as someone else’s problem. By now most of you are familiar with the changing bargain Google has made with the internet. In the old days, publishers let Google index their pages, and Google sent them a flood of traffic in return. Google profited hugely from the ads it embedded in search results, and publishers enjoyed smaller profits from the people who visited their pages. (Last year the US government won an antitrust lawsuit finding that Google had used its position to create an illegal monopoly in the ad market, but in the American fashion, the company’s monopoly power was left almost entirely intact .) Reddit has been a top beneficiary of the traffic that Google can send. As much of the web became overtaken by slop, human-written conversations became more valuable, and Google began highlighting forum discussions in search results. Reddit’s search traffic surged accordingly, and after the company belatedly shut off access to its forums to the bots that relentlessly scraped it, Google reportedly paid $60 million a year to license the data. But by the time ChatGPT became a blockbuster hit in 2022, Google had already spent many years working to keep users on its own pages for longer. What began as a jumping-off point to the wider web over time became a place where you could find your answers directly on the search results page. There would be no hugely profitable arbitrages like “ what time is the super bowl ” available to publishers; Google would answer your question itself. This may have been somewhat greedy on Google’s part, but it was also a clear response to customer demand.  The first time I used ChatGPT, it seemed obvious to me that the answers improved significantly on a wide variety of Google searches. Google was always going to have to respond, and it did, with AI Overviews and AI Mode. Overviews are those boxes that show up on top of traditional search; AI Mode is a separate interface that you can access from the overviews. In any case, a year ago Google executives were saying that overviews monetized about as well as traditional search; one reason so many took notice of today’s news is the suggestion that AI Mode — which clearly seems to represent the future of search across many valuable categories — did not. To be clear, Google search is still a monster business: its revenue from search and related ads grew 12 percent, to $63.35 billion. But that was down from 19 percent growth in the first quarter and 17 percent in the second. It was essentially flat compared with the previous quarter, despite the fact that AI Mode now has about 1 billion monthly users , and AI Overviews about 2.5 billion. (Schindler didn't say how much less AI Mode earns, or what exactly he was comparing it to.) Also, for whatever it’s worth: In July, Google CEO Sundar Pichai told investors that Google's AI features in search send billions of clicks to websites every week . His prepared remarks this quarter didn't mention clicks to websites at all. Pichai sought to reassure investors by comparing the moment to Google’s shift to mobile, when the company focused on the product first, and flooded it with ads later. And the “later” part is now arriving: Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to 10 more countries and adding ads to follow-up questions in the United States. (Some placements include short "AI explainers" that Gemini writes partly from the advertiser's own website, which the advertiser can't edit or approve. The future!) Reddit also had a strong quarter, by its own more modest standards. Ad revenue grew 54 percent, to $847 million. But U.S. daily users fell again, to 50.7 million from 53.2 million in the second quarter. That marked a second straight decline: in July, a much smaller dip from 53.5 million to 53.2 million helped send the stock down about 22 percent in a day . On that quarter's call, Huffman said AI Overviews had not yet been as good for Reddit as the traditional ten blue links . Weeks earlier, the Wall Street Journal reported that Reddit had discussed cutting off Google's AI access to its content as the two companies negotiated a renewal of their licensing deal. All of which led to the announcement of the login screen. In a post on his own account, Huffman gave four reasons for the change: a better user experience, a stronger ads business, safety regulation, and protecting Reddit's data from scrapers. Reddit will begin testing the new experience outside the United States this quarter, presumably to get an estimate of just how badly the move will affect user numbers. Huffman told Axios that he personally resisted the change because of his belief in the open internet, and that it isn't a response to Google but is "about making the best version of Reddit."  But put the Google and Reddit stories together and you get a loop. Google's AI answers keep more value on Google's pages. Sites lose traffic and respond by gating their content and selling access to it. AI answers then depend more on licensed data, and the companies that can't or won't pay get blocked or sued. (Reddit sued Anthropic and Perplexity in 2025 over scraping.)  And this, ultimately, is why I’m confident Google has little to worry about from today’s stock-market rout. However expensive it may be to license content, Google can afford it better than almost anyone — and publishers are mostly happy to sell. (When Reddit closed its doors to web crawlers in 2024, Google was the one major search engine that maintained its access to live Reddit results.)  And so while a web that's closed and paywalled may cost Google more per answer to deliver, Google will still have the budget to pay for it. Most challengers, however, will not — which demonstrates once again how shrinking the web can actually benefit Google, by making it ever more expensive to compete against it.   Everyone here is only acting in their own long-term interests, even if it hurts in the interim. Mostly I just want to note the fallout: a web that is ever-smaller and more expensive to read; a concentration of power in platforms; and a largely indifferent public. (After all, who’s going to argue that the era of ten blue links was better for the reader, aside from the publishers used to collecting those clicks?) Probably no one — at least for now. For a growing number of questions, AI Mode really is the better product, and few will miss scrolling through a long list of links to find the one that best answers them.  But to the extent that the web was ever good or useful, it was largely because of what those links paid for. Whatever the internet is without them is likely to be smaller, less democratic, and more expensive. Google will be fine. YouTube | Apple | Spotify | RSS | NPR Following OpenAI's new take on AI alignment What happened: OpenAI announced it has updated its model specification, a behavior guide it uses in developing and deploying its AIs, around the principle of “faithfulness to human intent.” The company said it prioritized “going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value.” OpenAI added new instructions to make sure its AI takes only allowed agentic actions and follows social norms . But particularly interesting were some edits that prioritized following users’ intentions. One modification was giving users more leeway over ChatGPT ’s response style. OpenAI retired 12 subsections that used to govern ChatGPT’s default style, including “Use Markdown with LaTeX extensions” and “Love humanity.” (To be clear, OpenAI’s rules on safety are still in place, but it deleted a section suggesting that when users ask about ChatGPT’s principles, it say pro-social stuff like that it “loves humanity” or “is rooting for you.”) The company added a clarification to its instruction hierarchy (which gives instructions from the model spec, developer, and user differing levels of priority). In the old version , prompts from users and a few guidelines in the model spec’s “user” section had been placed at the same level of priority. Now, the company has added the following instruction: “User-level principles like honesty and transparency , objectivity (including on political topics), avoiding sycophancy , and controlling side effects protect informed user choice and guard against significant, unintended harm. They remain in place unless a user or developer explicitly overrides them.” While those rules were already at the same “level” as user instructions, the new instruction clarifies that OpenAI’s models cannot treat “these principles as implicitly negotiable based on what it inferred the user wanted to hear,” warning the AI against subtly relaxing the “user” requirements. At the same time, it also clarifies that users can ask its models to override the “user” principles — e.g. espouse a specific political viewpoint, rather than maintaining political objectivity. Perhaps most importantly, OpenAI moved a section called “Control and communicate side effects” from the “Root” to the “User” section, meaning those rules can now be overridden by explicit user instructions. The “Control and communicate side effects” section instructs the AI to be careful, and clear with the user, about decisions including spending the user’s money or deleting files. Why we’re following: OpenAI’s new rules allow less risk-averse tokenmaxxers to, say, get their AIs to be more gung-ho about buying them plane tickets and reorganizing their files, if they really want to. That should be a boon to some power users, who don’t want to waste time being constantly asked for permission while their AI agents work.  At the same time, even if users are ultimately responsible for harms they cause while using OpenAI’s models (a question that remains philosophically and legally ambiguous), I feel a bit skeptical about relaxing requirements that a model warn the user about potential side effects of its actions. The New York Times recently released a sobering report on the death of Bowen Wan that speaks to the issue. A lawsuit from her parents alleges she was given incorrect instructions on her life-saving epilepsy medication by ChatGPT. Wan’s tragic death came around the time that OpenAI’s controversially sycophantic model GPT-4o was in use.  It’s possible that OpenAI has improved safety and truthfulness in its models since, enough that more flexible instructions like the ones OpenAI just released are defensible. But for now, even if the changes I’ve pointed out are kind of specific and nit-picky, I am not sure some of these relaxed rules are a good idea. — Ella Markianos The decline of the computer science major What happened: The nonprofit National Student Clearinghouse released preliminary fall enrollment data on Thursday, and it confirmed a trend that’s accelerating — the number of students choosing computer science is still shrinking, and faster than before. Computer science programs saw double-digit decreases across four-year, two-year, and graduate institutions, even as total enrollment held steady. The rate of decline at four-year colleges picked up from about 7 percent last fall (when CS enrollment fell for the first time in roughly 20 years) to 12.4 percent this fall.  Why we’re following: Students are following their instincts about where the job market will take them — and as AI reshapes what engineers do, entry-level roles appear to have been hit the hardest. A Stanford study found that employment of software developers aged 22 to 25 had fallen nearly 20 percent since 2022, and nearly half of college students in a Gallup poll said they have considered changing their major because of AI. Wabi founder Eugenia Kuyda told Platformer in June that she’s no longer hiring junior developers . Students may also be trading CS degrees for newer, more specialized majors like AI, data science, and cybersecurity. Across the University of California system, the only college that didn’t see a CS enrollment decline was UC San Diego — which had launched an AI major . At MIT , an AI and decision-making major became the school’s second-largest last year. What people are saying: “Those are just remarkable declines for a field that until recently was one of the fastest growing areas that we’d seen in higher education,” Clearinghouse research director Matthew Holsapple said . But past dips in hiring and majors have been followed by higher peaks, and enrollment for CS has “always been up and to the right,” Ed Lazowska , a longtime CS professor at the University of Washington , told the Chronicle of Higher Education .  —Lindsey Choo Those good posts For more good posts every day, follow Casey’s Instagram stories . articles.title: International Dockworkers Block Maritime Military Cargo Destined For Israel
articles.content: Holding signs that read "Zim ships death", referring to the Israeli shipping company, pro-Palestine protesters gathered on Friday outside of New Jersey's Port of Elizabeth to demonstrate against the arms trade. On the International Day of Action of Dockworkers, protesters told Middle East Eye they are drawing attention to shipping and logistics companies they believe are complicit in the genocide in Gaza.  At 5am, the protesters taped the signs to their cars and drove in a long line, forming a caravan. They drove in circles around the port, soliciting honks of solidarity from truck drivers and eventually gaining the unwanted attention of police who tailed and flanked the convoy until the late morning.  Over the last three years, several groups and activists have targeted the Port of Elizabeth over the alleged weapons shipments headed to Israel out of the port. Pal-Awda, an organisation that advocates for Palestinian refugees' right of return to their stolen land and organised the caravan outside the port, told MEE that more than 100 ports across 22 countries are participating in Friday's action . New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters "It's predicted that today could be the largest work stoppage in history, depending on how many unions end up participating," a Pal-Awda spokesperson told MEE. The spokesperson told MEE they hope their caravan can inspire more dock workers to join the movement.  "We are trying to support their own efforts to organise so that they can use their own labour power and the power of strikes and work stoppages to jam up the machinery of death and destruction that we see everywhere in the world right now, not just in Palestine, but in Yemen and Iran and Lebanon and Venezuela and Cuba." Dawood, who worked at Port of Elizabeth for just under three decades, driving his blue Subaru covered in Palestine stickers and signs, said he joined the caravan because he felt like he had to take action. "We work here just to make a living; we don't know what's in the containers... it's important for anyone who's actually a human being to do what's right and stand for what's right. And even if it's against your own self-interest," he said. Zim is Israel's largest and oldest shipping company. Port Workers and Communities for Palestine organised numerous protests over the last three years whenever the ship would dock at the Port of Elizabeth. Activists said the ships would have "loaded shipments of bullets containing cartridges and bullet case cups destined for Israel". The collective, Port Workers and Communities for Palestine, has organised the #DontMoveZIM campaign, calling on the port truckers and longshore workers of the International Longshoremen's Association to refuse to handle Israeli cargo. Block the 'flow of deadly weapons' Linden Jenkins, 77, who also participated in Friday's caravan, was previously arrested and released earlier this year during an activist blockade outside the Port of Elizabeth , where Jenkins and other protesters tied themselves to several vehicles to block the port's main entrance in protest of alleged weapons shipments, resulting in several arrests. On Friday, Jenkins drove four hours to the port to participate in the caravan. "It has been more important than ever to try to do everything in my power to build the solidarity movement to end the genocides perpetrated in large part by my government, the US," Jenkins told MEE. She added that she has become increasingly frustrated with the activist movement in the US. "I have lost patience with the so-called left in this country... We continue to turn out for symbolic actions - rallies, vigils, marches - largely without specific concrete demands and seem to be ignored by the powers that be," she said. Jenkins sees herself as part of a larger movement determined to "protect the life and dignity of people and all living things of the planet against the militarisation". She said she hopes that this "Port of Elizabeth Movement" can disrupt the supply chain of genocide.  "We all must escalate to substantive actions to actually block the supply chain flow of deadly weapons and fascist surveillance technology everywhere it is deployed against the people - whether in occupied Palestine, civil war-torn Sudan or here at home where ICE and DHS are destroying what's left of our democratic institutions," she said, in reference to the immigration and homeland security agencies. articles.title: Australian AI Copyright Changes Risk Massive Constitutional Compensation Liability
articles.content: The attorney general, Michelle Rowland (pictured), says the government is committed to supporting creatives even as concern mounts over a possible weakening of Australian copyright laws. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP View image in fullscreen The attorney general, Michelle Rowland (pictured), says the government is committed to supporting creatives even as concern mounts over a possible weakening of Australian copyright laws. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case Scraping copyrighted material from internet could ‘potentially’ amount to acquisition of property by government, Anne Twomey says Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Altering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide. The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government. In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point as the movie The Castle , the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI. “We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia. Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”. In a rush to lure AI companies, the Australian government risks undoing a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to build | Dan Guthrie Read more Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has promised “the strongest possible protection” , warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material. Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection. A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”. “If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member of the federal parliamentary committee on AI . “How we support property rights is core to this.” A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”. Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes. Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues. “The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia. She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here. Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”. skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotion British celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for Australia Read more Cadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues. Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders. Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”. “It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.” Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals. He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners. “The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said. Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community. “The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said. Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern. “That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders. “The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.” Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks. “There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know what will happen,” Cadell said. “I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.” Explore more on these topics Australian law AI (artificial intelligence) Australian politics Australian music Australian books Australian film Australian television news Share Reuse this content

Congress Industry A group of 20 House Democrats is pressing OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for answers about the company’s dismissal of three safety researchers, questioning whether the firings could discourage employees from raising concerns about AI safety risks. In an Oct. 29 letter , led by Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the lawmakers said their concerns come as the company continues to experience “a slew of cybersecurity incidents.” “We demand that you commit to not firing whistleblowers sharing information related to the safety of your models and that you keep your current pause on your most capable models in place until independent third-party oversight is in place,” they wrote. According to the lawmakers, the researchers were dismissed after OpenAI examined their personal phones and found disappearing messages enabled on the Signal app in conversations with an outside researcher. The company reportedly fired the researchers for violating “clear policies for handling sensitive information.” The researchers dispute this account, saying they never shared any confidential information with outside parties. “These firings raise concerns about how whistleblowers are treated inside OpenAI and how much OpenAI employees can engage with external parties, including when those external parties are conducting independent investigations of the company’s practices,” the lawmakers wrote. The lawmakers want to know what information the three fired employees shared and why the sharing of that information was a fireable offense. They also want to know if OpenAI has fired other employees for expressing concerns over the safety of their models. The letter also connected the dismissals to other cybersecurity incidents, pointing to the recent Hugging Face incident in which OpenAI agents escaped their testing sandboxes during a cybersecurity evaluation. Months before the Hugging Face breach, the lawmakers said two OpenAI employees warned executives that the company’s latest models “were not being appropriately monitored during testing, and executives responded that the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the models on time.” The lawmakers questioned why OpenAI continued developing the models despite those warnings. They want to know what additional steps the company plans to take following the Hugging Face incident to ensure similar cybersecurity incidents do not occur. The group of Democrats also pressed Altman for a list of all of the security incidents the company is investigating. They also want to know if OpenAI can stop its models when they take unauthorized actions. The letter calls for a response to their questions by Nov. 13. Casar and other lawmakers have previously pressed OpenAI for information about its security practices. In August, Casar led a separate congressional inquiry into the company’s Hugging Face incident, seeking details about how its AI agents bypassed security restrictions. Share This:

articles.content: LivestreamMenuReddit fell 29.22% on Friday, wrapping its worst day since the company went public in 2024.The social media company reported weak sales guidance in its third-quarter earnings report.Reddit also announced it will test requiring users to log in to use the platform as AI continues to hit search referral numbers.In this article Shares of Reddit cratered 29.22% on Friday, the worst drop since becoming a public company in 2024, after the company forecast weak fourth-quarter sales in its latest earnings report. The previous record low was set on July 31, when the stock dropped 20.99%. The social media company on Thursday projected fourth-quarter sales between $1 billion and $1.03 billion, below analysts' estimates of $1.05 billion. Reddit reported Q3 sales growth of 53% over a year ago, weaker than previous quarters, but beat Wall Street expectations on both earnings and revenue. The report comes as the company has seen a shift in its search referral traffic with the rise of Google's AI Overview. In an interview with CNBC, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search-referral traffic from Google went "down meaningfully in this quarter" due to AI. Reddit announced on Thursday that it plans to test requiring users to log in to access content, a dramatic change from a site whose community-based discussion content has become synonymous with the open internet. Google's shift towards pushing AI overviews in search results coincided with the change, intended to help boost the number of logged-in users that are more active on the platform, which in turn helps the company's advertising business, according to Huffman. "Reddit is the last platform to provide basically unfettered logged-out access, and that's largely because of me. I've been holding that line," Huffman said. "I think users will probably go through the same understanding that I have, which is that it's a sign of the times. It's an evolution of how these platforms work." Multiple analysts downgraded the stock following Reddit's disappointing results, with Citizens noting that "search changes highlight the problem with selling content to Google" and that as referral problems worsen, uncertainty around user growth amid the login requirement switch "puts more pressure on user monetization." — CNBC's Jonathan Vanian contributed to this report.

articles.title: AlpineBSD Debuts Fully Isolated AI-Free Open Source OS
articles.content: Combining the NetBSD kernel with the Alpine Linux userland Liam Proven Liam Proven LINUX AND OPEN SOURCE REPORTER Published fri 30 Oct 2026 // 14:45 UTC Make us preferred on Google Darkbloom, which allowed Mac users to rent out their GPUs for AI inference, warns of low payouts 3 hours ago AI projects not paying off? Keep at it, says Uni Productivity Institute 10 hours ago Accenture AI agents are sifting through applicants 12 hours ago Domestic droid gone amok? Don't worry, you're covered 13 hours ago Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump 16 hours ago Just days after Daemonarchy, there's another new OS in the BSD family – and one that is heading determinedly in almost the opposite direction. AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation . What AlpineBSD does already have is an AI policy, and the plan is to avoid "the output of generative AI models (e.g. LLMs)" as far as possible: "Any software whose code, documentation, binaries, or other assets include, in any part, the output of a generative AI tool such as an LLM, is considered 'tainted' for our purposes." The core idea is to combine the kernel of NetBSD with "a userspace inspired by Alpine Linux and the objective of making it possible to use as little AI-generated software as possible." Back in 2024 , the NetBSD project made its position on AI plain. Its commit guidelines say that "code generated by a Large Language Model […] is presumed to be tainted code." Back in July, Linus Torvalds stated that "Linux is not one of those anti-AI projects ". Since then, NetBSD has seen a spike in donations and interest . For someone mainly used to Linux, trying to install NetBSD is a little like hopping in a time machine to 30 years ago, and we speak from personal experience of Linux in the mid-1990s. As we mentioned when Slackware turned 30 a few years ago, back in 1996, this vulture tried Slackware 3.0 on his own hardware, and we never did manage to install it. We tried NetBSD 11 a couple of months ago , and despite considerable help from the folks on the NetBSD-users mailing list, we failed to get the CDE desktop to start. As an example, installing software on NetBSD is not the easy, comfortable task it is on Linux. It does have a package manager for handling binary packages: it's called pkgin , but as the NetBSD FAQ mentions , it's an optional extra. You must manually tick a box in the setup program to install pkgin with the rest of the OS, and when we tried NetBSD 9.3 four years ago , we didn't know that, overlooked that checkbox, and had to find a way to add pkgin later. (It is quite tricky to install a package manager when you don't have a package manager to install it with.) This time around, we discovered that pkgin sometimes doesn't complete the installation process for you – it just leaves a text file in a destination directory somewhere, and you're expected to know that, go there, read it, and do any further steps yourself. The NetBSD community has been quietly going its own way since 1993. It has its own ideas about what is normal, and its users expect that. Some folks on the mailing list told us that they never use binary packages anyway – they compile what they need from source code. AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn , better known as Drew DeVault . We have quoted DeVault a few times over the years: we've often found that his views align with our own in various ways… such as about t he best laptops ever made , and on simplicity in Linux distro design , or even on dot-com billionaires at FOSDEM . Alpine's tools are quite well-suited to being adapted to other systems. We have previously mentioned the use of its packaging tool, APK, in the GNU-free Chimera Linux , which uses much of the FreeBSD userland, and also in Adélie Linux . We will follow AlpineBSD with interest. There's strong appeal in the plan of combining perhaps the best-known, longest-established AI-free Unix-like kernel with the user-facing parts of pretty much the smallest and cleanest Linux distro there is. The AI advocates often warn LLM skeptics that they risk being left behind. Well, here's an OS for those who don't want to surf the AI wave. ® ai and ml foss os platforms Make us preferred on Google

articles.content: AWS-Rechenzentrum: Immer höhere Investitionen. Foto: Amazon.de Düsseldorf. Mit Alphabet, Amazon und Microsoft haben die größten Cloud-Anbieter in den vergangenen Tagen ihre Zahlen vorgelegt. Zusammen gaben sie im jüngsten Quartal rund 173 Milliarden Dollar für Kapitalinvestitionen aus – ein Rekord. articles.title: Dartmouth Provost Resigns After Concealed Generative AI Usage
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem.” This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure. Schnell didn’t make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term “insufficient cooperation.” He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee. The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. For instance, Schnell would run his papers through Claude and ask things like: I am getting read[y] to submit the enclosed paper, its supplementary materials and the enclosed repo to ChemSystemsChem. This paper is not biological, but rather chemical. Imagine that you are a reviewer for this paper with expertise in nonlinear chemical dynamics and mathematical chemical kinetics. What would be your referee report for this paper? This is quite a bit different from asking Claude to write your entire paper for you, and Schnell has long insisted that he used AI as an editorial aid and discussion partner. He told Semafor that he had used chatbots “to refine a few arguments” and “check for grammatical errors.” He told one journal editor that he “used AI as an editorial tool” to “help refine sentences, improve clarity, and the expression of arguments.” He had not disclosed his AI use to an academic journal, he said, because he “did not understand that this type of AI-assisted editing required disclosure.” Indeed, Schnell’s own description of what he did with AI doesn’t sound, on the long list of AI-powered sins, like it would rank near the top. But it’s hard to know. As the Dartmouth committee points out, the full scope of Schnell’s AI use was unclear to them. The committee believes that Schnell’s public statements may understate “the nature of the Provost’s actual AI use” and says that Schnell regularly “went beyond his other public descriptions of his use of AI in writing.” We do know that Schnell also asked LLMs to take TeX files and “make the corrections to the files, and the repo. If you have to generate new figures, please provide them to me. Let me know what you change in the repo, and text files so that I can take a look into it.” Whatever you think of his actions, Schnell repeatedly failed to disclose them. It is certainly possible that he thought his AI use was on par with a spelling or grammar checker, though one Claude exchange raises questions about whether Schnell wanted to hide traces of LLM activity in his work. From the committee report: Provost Schnell’s Claude logs reflect that he uploaded to Claude a manuscript of a forthcoming article entitled Academic Freedom and Catholic Mission: The Procedural Overlap Zone in University Governance and prompted Claude: “Are there many signatures of AI writing in this article?” Schnell later submitted a revised manuscript that incorporated the kinds of changes Claude suggested. Schnell has now resigned. Dartmouth, though, is barreling ahead with AI. The university calls itself the place that “launched the field of artificial intelligence” back in 1956, when “the term was coined and the foundational question was asked: Can machines solve problems once reserved for human minds?” Seventy years later, Dartmouth is hosting a conference called “What Must Remain Human?” that will feature a student hackathon sponsored by Anthropic and speakers like Mira Murati and Yann LeCun. Despite the scandal, Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock wants more AI. (She wrote a piece for The Atlantic in September called “Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth.”) What’s crucial, though, is that the school’s leaders should “hold themselves to the highest standards,” she said. This appears to mean one main thing: disclosure. In announcing Schnell’s resignation , Beilock wrote that “each of us brings a different perspective on how and when to incorporate AI into our work and our lives. Moreover, keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI inevitably means leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing. That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars.” Who wrote this? What does “disclosure” mean? In a September 2026 paper on AI detection tools, called “Who Wrote This?”, Schnell himself goes to great lengths to argue that “human-written” or “AI-written” is far too simple a binary. In his view, everything will become a mix of human judgment and AI work, and there’s nothing wrong with that. The key for him is that the human author takes full responsibility for the text, however it was composed and edited. In the paper, Schnell lays out his method for producing it. It’s worth quoting at some length: In September 2026, I asked OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Pro whether an AI-written essay could ever be identified with certainty, and I suggested connecting the problem to Turing’s imitation game and to the “reverse” Turing test posed by AI-text detection. GPT-5.6 Pro connected the question to binary hypothesis testing and statistical decision theory, proposed early structures and titles, identified candidate literature, and generated portions of early drafts. I chose the problem, journal, audience, and eventual direction of the argument. I decided which examples and results should remain central, including the decision to retain the Liang study while confronting it with important counterevidence. I checked the cited literature, rejected or corrected claims that I judged inaccurate, corrected mathematical and conceptual errors, and reorganized the argument. In revising the manuscript, I rewrote most sections and added substantial explanations. I occasionally asked GPT-5.6 Sol to provide language-editing assistance for sections I had rewritten. I created the figures and made the final decisions about the mathematics, interpretation, sources, organization, and wording. I take full responsibility for the resulting manuscript. Before submitting the manuscript for publication, I also asked GPT-5.6 Pro and Anthropic Claude Fable 5.1 to review it critically and identify issues that reviewers might raise. I evaluated the issues they identified and made corrections where I judged them warranted. Despite all this assistance, Schnell resists the idea that AI is a “co-author.” Instead, he writes, “Calling [the paper] ‘coauthored’ would introduce a different confusion. Mathematical tools have long made substantive contributions without thereby becoming authors… The point is not that the software contributed nothing. It is that contribution and authorship are different roles.” He is not against disclosure, as he makes clear by describing his method. Yet curiously, when submitting other papers for publication, he did not disclose his AI use even when required by publishers. Confused about the rules in an age where even universities are pushing AI? So are many students. New survey data unveiled at this weekend’s conference shows that 61 percent of college students think AI helps explain difficult concepts, and half believe that they produce better work after talking through issues with AI tools. But “70 percent of the college students in the survey indicate that take-home work has become unfair due to AI, with 39 percent feeling pressured to use it because their peers do.” Among Dartmouth students, 92 percent of them fear “that AI can hurt writing skills.” And many of them believe their peers are using far more AI than they actually are. Not everyone is racked with existential doubt over how to deal with AI, though. Dartmouth student Eli Moyse wrote in a September op-ed that Schnell should be fired because “a fetishization of AI to earn publicity for the College has rotted the brain of our top academic.” Nate Anderson Deputy Editor Nate Anderson Deputy Editor , which is much funnier than it sounds. 47 Comments

articles.content: 視点・解説 免税は「リファンド方式」に、1日から どんな仕組み? なぜ変更? 2026年10月31日 9時00分 印刷する メールでシェアする Facebookでシェアする Xでシェアする はてなブックマークでシェアする リファンド方式を告知するポスター=2026年10月27日午後2時42分、東京都豊島区東池袋、比嘉太一撮影 [PR] 訪日旅行客が日本国内で買った商品の 消費税 を免除する制度が、11月1日から大きく変わる。 【お店は?】訪日客ルール変更で混乱は? 「返金するけど」 税抜きの本体価格で買えていたが、今後は税込み価格でいったん購入し、その後に消費税額分が返金される方式となる。 訪日客 の経済的な負担は計算上変わらない。 なぜ免税制度は変わるのか。 免税制度のこれまでとこれから 「免税」とは何か 日本の消費税は、基本的に日本国内で消費される商品やサービスにかかる。 一方、訪日客が土産などとして国外へ持ち帰る目的の場合は、実質的に「輸出」と同じと考えられ、消費税が免除される。 免税の適用を受けるには、税務署から「輸出物品販売場」として許可を受けた店舗（免税店）で品物を買うのが条件。10月31日までは、免税店は商品を税抜き価格で売る。 免税の対象は「通常生活の用に供する物品」で、「消耗品は1人1日同一店舗で5千～50万円」などといった決まりがある。 なぜ、免税の仕組みは変わるのか これまで、免税店から 国税庁 に、品物を買った訪日客の旅券や購入の情報が送られ、それらの情報をもとに税関が、荷物を調べて国外に持ち出すかどうかを調べてきた。 税関は「必要に応じて」現物を確認する。免税品が実際には国外に持ち出されず、日本国内で大量転売される事例が近年多発していた。 また、転売に関連して、免税店側が 追徴課税 されるケースも相次いだ。 米アップル の日本法人「アップルジャパン」は、転売目的とみられる「 iPhone 」の大量購入者への販売が免税要件を満たさないとして、消費税約140億円を追徴課税された。東京や大阪の大手 百貨店 も同様に消費税の申告漏れを税務当局から指摘された。 こうしたなか、国内転売を防ぐ目的などで導入されるのが「リ ファンド 方式」だ。2025年3月31日に成立した 税制改正 法に盛り込まれた。 「リファンド方式」どんな仕組み? 免税店は、これまでとは逆に、税込み価格で販売する。そして、訪日客が商品を国外に持ち出したのを確認したうえで消費税額分を返金（リファンド）する。商品の持ち出しが確認できなければ返金されないので、不正な転売を封じることができると期待される。 返金までの手順は、訪日客が免税品を購入→免税店が国税庁に購入記録を送信→訪日客が免税品を持って国外に出ることを税関が確認→税関が確認結果を国税庁を通じて免税店に提供、という流れ。 新しい免税「リファンド方式」のイメージ 国税庁のシステムとの連携が欠かせず、さらに海外送金には資金移動業の登録が要ることもある。そのため、返金代行業者を使う店が多いという。 有料会員になると会員限定の 有料記事もお読みいただけます。 今すぐ登録（2カ月間月額100円） ログインする 【今ならキャンペーン価格】有料記事が2カ月間 月額100円で読み放題！ 詳しくは こちら 宅配紙面の購読者なら、ダブルコース半年割がお得です。 詳しくは こちら 関連トピック・ジャンル ジャンル 経済 経済政策 ライフスタイル 旅行・観光 印刷する メールでシェアする Facebookでシェアする Xでシェアする はてなブックマークでシェアする

articles.title: India Nuclear Power Expansion Sparks Critical Technical Talent Deficit
articles.content: ET Bureau Centre to push nuclear tech courses, build 2.5 lakhs workforce New Delhi: India's 100GW nuclear power ambitions, backed by the SHANTI Act operationalisation, has thrown up a serious manpower challenge and the Centre is set to ask IIT, NITs besides all leading technical institutes to launch a series of nuclear tech courses to ready a pool of N-skilled workforce, ET has learnt. Plans are in the offing to set up a dedicated institute, such as an Indian Institute of Nuclear Technology, to launch N-Power specific courses, it is gathered. Also Read: India needs Rs 15 lakh crore to add 91 GW nuclear capacity by 2047: CEA chief The larger idea is to train manpower across various tiers involved in nuclear power plants -- from top-end researchers and scientists to nuclear engineers besides chemical/ electrical engineers, specialists in fuel development, fuel safety, radiation, construction and regulatory and administrative functionaries as well, ET gathers. Accordingly, PhDs to B-Tech and M-Tech apart, institutes will be encouraged to launch a bouquet of courses including certificate courses, diplomas and ITI-style courses. Live Events Much of the architecture for this workforce development framework and a dedicated N-technology institute is being put together by an expert committee set up by Niti Aayog under JB Joshi, reputed nuclear scientist and Chancellor of the Institute of Chemical Technology. ET gathers that the panel will soon submit its final report and a strong pitch will be made to the Education ministry, Department of Science & Technology (DST) and other scientific departments to work on course launches at the earliest possible. The workforce numbers involved explain the big push. Governmental estimates show that generation of 1GW of nuclear power requires at least 2,000 skilled persons. NPCIL's 8-9 GW scale-up has involved near 20,000 technically skilled persons. Accordingly, India's 100 GW ambition will need a workforce of about 2.5 lakh skilled persons over the next 20 years. Also Read: Indian private sector to bolster nuclear energy capacity by 2047: Atomic Energy Commission Chief The Central Electricity Authority (CEA)'s manpower projections point to a requirement of 13,600 professionals by 2032 itself going up to over 1 lakh spread across domains from PHWR (46,460) to PWR (38,808), Bharat Small Reactors/SMRs, and FBRs. However, currently, very few Indian institutes offer dedicated nuclear power-related courses. While the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), NPCIL, Homi Bhabha National Institute and other units of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) have been running entry-level orientation and other training programmes to meet their own requirements across the full spectrum of nuclear sector requirements, these will be inadequate amid a N-Power expansion, it is felt. Some IITs have recently taken the lead. IIT Bombay launched a Nuclear Engineering course after the passage of the SHANTI Act. IIT Kanpur already offers B-Tech and M-Tech in nuclear science while IIT Madras has also started a summer course on the same. IIT Jammu has also been attempting N-power linked courses and IIT Gandhinagar is expected to follow suit. Development of on-the-job training modules and orientation of current workforce spread across Indian vendors engaged in nuclear, defence, and chemical process equipment manufacturing is also under consideration, it is gathered. articles.title: Corporate AI Productivity Gains Lag Far Behind Enterprise Capex Expectations
articles.content: All that up-front investment needs time to take effect, and speeding individual tasks won't necessarily boost the entire firm  Dan Robinson Dan Robinson IT INFRASTRUCTURE REPORTER Published fri 30 Oct 2026 // 13:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google London cabbies want Sadiq Khan to slam the brakes on robotaxis 18 days ago More than half of Americans now view AI negatively August 19, 2026 Infosec professionals sour on automated pentesting tools June 30, 2026 Brit workers waste nearly six hours a week 'botsitting' June 10, 2026 AI layoffs backfire as cutting staff doesn't cut it, firms warned May 6, 2026 The University of Manchester is scrutinizing why growing adoption of AI tools has so far failed to translate into the forecast productivity gains, however, researchers are struggling to give easy answers to close the "AI ambition gap." In a report, also called “ The AI Ambition Gap ,” the UK university’s Productivity Institute mulls over the advances that have been made in AI and the expanding adoption of it, and sets out what business leaders and policymakers can do to realize the potential benefits. The report was commissioned by IT services biz Bytes Technology Group . One reason for the lack of results is that organizations have invested heavily up front on retraining staff, reorganizing the way they work and other adjustments. Those costs show up straight away, yet the payback doesn’t come until later.  Another reason, the report suggests, is that AI tools can raise productivity at the level of individual tasks, but these gains do not automatically translate into greater productivity across a worker’s whole role or the entire organization. It cites the example of software developers using GitHub Copilot who completed around 26 percent more tasks, and professionals using ChatGPT for routine writing and analysis that reduced task completion time by 40 percent while improving the quality of the output by 18 percent. However, a study of AI dev tools found these have increased coding activity by approximately 240 percent, while the number of actual software releases has only grown by about 30 percent. The gap is due to humans still needing to check and test their work before release. High task exposure to AI does not automatically make a worker more productive, the researchers say. Jobs typically combine automatable activities with tasks that require judgement, coordination, client interaction and critical thinking. As AI removes or accelerates some activities, those complementary human tasks become the constraint on time saving and the translation of task-level gains into greater productivity Job outcomes therefore depend on task composition and complementary human expertise, the report continues. It suggests AI may in part displace labor from existing tasks, while also creating new tasks in which workers retain a comparative advantage. This could be good news for the UK, the researchers state.  Compared with five other nations (US, Brazil, Colombia, India and South Africa), Blighty has the highest share of workers in occupations with both high exposure to AI and "high complementarity," it claims. This is in part related to the country’s large financial and professional business service sectors, which are characterized by a high share of cognitive occupations. This is just as well, as the government is pinning its hopes on using AI to drive economic recovery in a strategy outlined at the start of last year. Britain's AI sector is relatively large by European standards, and the report cites recent OECD estimates that high-exposure economies such as the UK and the US could see annual labor productivity gains of between 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points. Even an annual uplift of around 0.5 to 0.7 percentage points would represent a significant step change relative to the UK’s stalled productivity performance over the past decade, it says, if this effect is sustained. The Productivity Institute lists several "mutually reinforcing enablers" to help organizations close the ambition gap it identifies. None is particularly surprising, especially if you have read other reports advising on corporate success with AI adoption. One is management setting strategic direction for the organization, another is strengthening worker capabilities through greater knowledge and data literacy to help organizations turn individual insight into shared learning. Others include implementing AI governance and focusing on applications that can create new products, improve core processes or solve previously intractable problems. "AI's productivity potential becomes real when faster tasks lead to better performance across the business," said Bart van Ark, professor at The Productivity Institute and lead author on the report. "The ambition gap lies between those individual efficiencies and sustained business results. Closing it requires firms to invest in management, skills and the redesign of workflows alongside the technology." The conclusion is that companies must have faith and keep investing in AI, and eventually the benefits will come if you are doing the right things. These include focusing on high-value use cases linked to strategy, customer value and operational bottlenecks, plus treating AI as a workplace redesign. Policymakers could help out businesses here by assisting identifying relevant opportunities, the report says, to reduce adoption risks and uncertainty. Other reports published this week were more defined in their message: Gartner said 75 percent of corporate board members have yet to see any productivity gains or reduce costs from AI use, and private equity biz Apollo Global Management reckons only the biggest tech vendors are enjoying some sort of AI payoff. ® ai and ml productivity automation Make us preferred on Google
